source_first_audit.profile_reason: The headword combines high-frequency range and opportunity senses with separate planning, observation, logic, programming, and instrument uses.

coverage_axes.notes: Opportunity, range, purpose, nautical, instrument, logic, observation, planning, and programming senses are inventoried; rare source senses are explicitly excluded by union disposition.
Noun frames include scope for and within/beyond/outside scope; verb frames cover scope something, scope a project, and scope out.
The inventory records inflected verb forms and the productive phrasal form scope out.
Logic, linguistics, optical instruments, JavaScript scope, and Python name-resolution uses are covered.
Dictionary labels and usage notes distinguish core noun senses from informal scope out and technical uses.
Pronunciation and the Italian/Greek etymological path are recorded.

facts.statement: Scope is the opportunity or ability to do or achieve something.
facts.source_detail: The noun entry defines scope as opportunity or ability and gives scope for patterns.

facts.statement: Scope is the range of subjects an organization, activity, book, or investigation deals with.
facts.source_detail: The noun entry defines the range of things a subject, organization, or activity deals with.

facts.statement: Scope for introduces an opportunity or room for an action or development.
facts.source_detail: The entry explicitly lists scope for and scope for somebody to do something.

facts.statement: Within scope, beyond scope, and outside scope locate an activity relative to a defined range.
facts.source_detail: The entry gives within/beyond/outside somebody's scope as common patterns.

facts.statement: The headword is pronounced UK /skəʊp/ and US /skoʊp/.
facts.source_detail: The learner pronunciation convention identifies the vowel difference by region.

facts.statement: Informally, to scope something is to look at or examine it carefully.
facts.source_detail: The verb entry labels this use informal and defines it as looking at or examining carefully.

facts.statement: To scope a project or task is to examine it before work begins to understand its size and requirements.
facts.source_detail: The entry describes examining a project before starting work so its size is known.

facts.statement: The verb inflects as scope, scopes, scoped, and scoping.
facts.source_detail: The entry's grammar box lists the regular third-person, past, and -ing forms.

facts.statement: Scope can denote an intention, object, or purpose.
facts.source_detail: The dictionary includes intention or object among noun senses; this is retained as an excluded source candidate.

facts.statement: Scope can denote space or opportunity for action.
facts.source_detail: The noun senses include space or opportunity for action or thought.

facts.statement: Scope can denote the extent of treatment, activity, or influence.
facts.source_detail: The noun entry defines scope as the extent of a treatment, activity, or influence.

facts.statement: In logic or grammar, scope is the range over which an operator or constituent has effect.
facts.source_detail: The entry includes logical operator and grammatical constituent uses.

facts.statement: A scope can be an optical instrument such as a telescope, endoscope, or rifle scope.
facts.source_detail: The countable instrument senses include telescope, endoscope, and a rifle scope.

facts.statement: To scope out is to look over or evaluate a person, place, or possibility; scope can also mean examine with an optical instrument or equip a weapon.
facts.source_detail: The verb entry includes scope out, telescope/endoscope examination, and equipping a rifle with a scope.

facts.statement: The noun comes through Italian scopo from Greek skopos, a watching or aim-related noun.
facts.source_detail: The dictionary etymology traces scope through Italian to Greek skopos.

facts.statement: Scope can mean opportunity, capacity, or room for action.
facts.source_detail: The entry gives opportunity and capacity as noun senses.

facts.statement: Scope can mean the range or area of application or operation.
facts.source_detail: The noun entry covers range, area, application, and operation.

facts.statement: In nautical use, scope can mean the slack or length of anchor cable paid out.
facts.source_detail: The entry records this specialized nautical sense; it is retained as an excluded source candidate.

facts.statement: In logic and linguistics, scope is the range over which a word or operator has effect.
facts.source_detail: The entry explicitly lists logic and linguistics usage.

facts.statement: Scope is also used as a short form for an optical instrument.
facts.source_detail: The entry records the short form and instrument use.

facts.statement: As an American informal verb, scope means to look at, read, or investigate.
facts.source_detail: The verb entry labels this use American informal and gives look/read/investigate meanings.

facts.statement: In programming, scope is the current execution context in which values and expressions are visible or can be referenced.
facts.source_detail: MDN defines scope as the current context of execution and visibility of values and expressions.

facts.statement: Programming scopes can be layered; a child scope can access a parent scope, but a parent cannot access a child scope.
facts.source_detail: MDN describes nested scopes and the direction of visibility between them.

facts.statement: JavaScript includes global, module, function, and block scopes.
facts.source_detail: MDN lists the main JavaScript scope categories.

facts.statement: In Python, a scope defines the visibility of a name within a block.
facts.source_detail: The execution model states that a scope defines the visibility of names within a block.

facts.statement: Python resolves a name by searching the nearest enclosing scope according to its name-resolution rules.
facts.source_detail: The execution model explains lookup through the nearest enclosing scope.

facts.statement: Python distinguishes local, global, and free-variable bindings when describing name resolution.
facts.source_detail: The execution model distinguishes local, global, and free variables in a code block.

source_union.canonical_statement: Scope is available room or opportunity for action or achievement.
source_union.rationale: This central modern uncountable noun sense is represented by definition 1 and its frames.

source_union.canonical_statement: Scope is the range or extent covered by a subject, activity, investigation, application, or influence.
source_union.rationale: This central noun sense is represented by definition 2 and boundary contrasts.

source_union.canonical_statement: Scope for expresses opportunity, while within, beyond, and outside scope position an activity relative to a boundary.
source_union.rationale: These recurrent noun frames are required for usable English and are represented in grammar patterns.

source_union.canonical_statement: Informally, scope or scope out means to look over, investigate, or evaluate something.
source_union.rationale: The article separates the informal inspection verb from project planning.

source_union.canonical_statement: To scope a project or task is to examine and define it before work begins.
source_union.rationale: The planning and requirements-management verb is common in business and technical contexts.

source_union.canonical_statement: The verb has the regular forms scopes, scoped, and scoping.
source_union.rationale: The article records the inflectional family without treating it as a separate lexical sense.

source_union.canonical_statement: A scope can be an optical viewing instrument, including a telescope, endoscope, or rifle scope.
source_union.rationale: The countable instrument sense is standard and supports distinct collocations.

source_union.canonical_statement: In logic and linguistics, scope is the range over which an operator or expression has effect.
source_union.rationale: This specialist noun use is distinct from ordinary subject-range scope and is included as a technical extension.

source_union.canonical_statement: Scope is pronounced /skəʊp/ in UK English and /skoʊp/ in US English, and traces through Italian to Greek.
source_union.rationale: Pronunciation and etymology are explicit article sections and are source-grounded.

source_union.canonical_statement: In programming, scope is the visibility context governing names and expressions, with nested language-specific rules.
source_union.rationale: The article includes a bounded programming sense with JavaScript and Python examples.

source_union.canonical_statement: Scope may denote intention, object, or purpose in a dictionary sense.
source_union.rationale: This historical or less productive synonymic extension is recorded as a source candidate but not given a separate modern learner sense.

source_union.canonical_statement: Scope has a specialized nautical sense for the slack or length of anchor cable paid out.
source_union.rationale: This specialized nautical sense is outside the bounded standard learner profile and not productive in the target contexts.
